title: Warm Marches lowered late-March feeder reports of departing winter-visitor birds in eastern North America in 2002-2024, but the pre-registered all-species test was null
abstract: Question: do short-distance migrant birds that winter at feeders leave earlier after a warm March? We used Project FeederWatch checklists (seasons 2002-2024), NOAA GHCN_CAMS March temperature, and Breeding Bird Survey data to remove breeding areas. Retention is the reporting rate of a winter-visitor species in 15-31 March divided by its rate in mid-winter at the same sites, minus the same value for resident feeder birds in the same 2-degree cell and season. The analysis plan was written before the models. Over all 356 species-cells, the March slope did not differ clearly from zero in any of four samples (East and West, 2002-2012 and 2013-2024); the pre-registered test failed. Most species-cells (for example Dark-eyed Junco and White-throated Sparrow) do not decrease before 31 March, so the common window could not detect their departure. In an exploratory subset of species-cells that decrease during March, a 1 C warmer March lowered retention in the East by 4.1% (95% interval 1.8 to 7.4) in 2002-2012 and 3.1% (1.1 to 5.0) in 2013-2024, about 3.5 days earlier per 1 C (2.3 to 5.1). Next- and previous-season placebos, a snow control, and removal of insectivores did not remove the East result. West estimates were negative but uncertain. Retention had no clear 2002-2024 trend, and March did not warm clearly at the sites. Limitations: the subset was chosen after the main test; lower reports can mean less feeder use, not departure; species that leave in April were not testable.

display.caption: A: Change in late-March retention of winter-visitor birds relative to resident feeder birds per 1 C March anomaly (100 x log ratio, about percent; 95% season-bootstrap intervals). Top: pre-registered test on all 356 species-cells. Bottom: exploratory subset of species-cells whose reporting rate decreases during March. Circles 2002-2012, squares 2013-2024; blue East, orange West. B: Placebo check for the exploratory subset. The current March anomaly gives a negative slope in the East; next and previous seasons' anomalies give smaller slopes with intervals that include zero.

Left: Per-species March temperature slopes of relative log retention, 2002-2024, with season-bootstrap intervals. Species that leave in March (American Tree Sparrow, Ruby-crowned Kinglet, Yellow-rumped Warbler) have negative slopes; Dark-eyed Junco and White-throated Sparrow have near-zero slopes with narrow intervals. Right: Mean relative log retention per species-cell against the cell's 1991-2020 March climate.

Season effects (species-cell fixed effects) of relative log retention (top) and of the March temperature anomaly at the same cells (bottom), East and West, 2002-2024. Neither series has a clear linear trend.

citations.reason: Prior campaign result on FeederWatch winter community temperature index; we use its data choices (VALID flag, East/West split at -100, GHCN_CAMS) and add a departure-timing test.
Related campaign result: winter feeder communities changed toward warm species faster than breeding communities.
